cues.text: An Exile's Daughter
Margaret was born around 1045 in Hungary, where her father, Edward the Exile, had been raised after fleeing England as an infant during the political upheavals following the Danish conquest.
When Edward was finally summoned home as a possible heir to the English throne, he died almost immediately upon arrival.
His young family — Margaret, her sister Christina, and her brother Edgar the Aetheling — grew up at the English court.
Edgar was the last plausible Anglo-Saxon claimant to England's crown, under the protection of their great-uncle, King Edward the Confessor.

Their security did not last: after the Norman Conquest of 1066, the family fled north, and a storm, tradition says, drove their ship to the coast of Scotland rather than the continent they had intended.
A Reluctant Queen

Margaret had reportedly hoped for a life of religious dedication rather than marriage, but King Malcolm III of Scotland, struck by her piety and bearing, pressed his suit, and around 1070 she became his queen.
The marriage proved a genuine partnership.
Margaret's influence softened a court that chroniclers describe as rough and unlettered.
Malcolm, though himself only modestly literate, is said to have had her devotional books bound in jeweled covers out of sheer admiration for what she read in them.
Together they raised eight children, several of whom would themselves become kings and queens of Scotland and England.
Reform From the Throne

As queen, Margaret used her position deliberately in service of the Church, convening a synod that corrected irregularities in the observance of Lent and Easter and worked to align Scottish ecclesiastical practice more closely with the wider Latin Church.
She founded the Abbey of Dunfermline to house a relic of the True Cross she treasured above all her other possessions.

She personally served the poor and orphaned rather than simply funding their care from a distance—feeding beggars with her own hands and washing the feet of the destitute during Lent and Advent, a practice her husband joined her in.
Four Days of Grief
In November 1093 King William Rufus of England launched a surprise attack on the castle of Alnwick; Malcolm and the couple's eldest son, Edward, were both killed in the fighting.

Margaret, already gravely ill, received the news at Edinburgh Castle and died four days later, on 16 November 1093, her final words, by her biographer Turgot's account, a prayer of thanksgiving even in the depth of her grief.
Legacy

Pope Innocent IV canonized Margaret in 1250, citing her personal holiness, her fidelity to the Church, and her tireless charity toward the poor, and in 1673 she was declared patroness of Scotland outright.
We recognize in Margaret a queen who never let the demands of a royal household excuse her from the harder, messier work of charity.

She understood, centuries before anyone wrote it down as a principle, that reforming a kingdom from the throne meant nothing if it wasn't matched by kneeling, personally, before the poorest people in it.
